#Deploy

#Files

The control page is plain files in public/ — Vue 3, xterm, the Ace editor and CodeMirror are vendored, nothing is built at run time. After npm install, run bin/vendor once to copy them out of node_modules into public/vendor/ (the copies also live in the repo); CodeMirror comes as many small modules, so bin/vendor bundles it into one file with esbuild.

#Hostnames

Every service needs a name that resolves to the serviceman host. One wildcard record is usually enough:

*.example.com.    A    203.0.113.10

*.localhost resolves to 127.0.0.1 on most systems, which is why the config in the repo uses it.

#Port 80

Ports below 1024 need a privilege. Pick one:

setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' $(which node)     # let node bind 80 directly
# or keep 8080 and put nginx, caddy or a tunnel in front

#TLS

serviceman speaks plain HTTP. For HTTPS, put a TLS terminator in front of it (caddy, nginx, cloudflare) and send everything to serviceman with the Host header untouched. serviceman adds x-forwarded-for, x-forwarded-proto and x-forwarded-host for the service behind it.

#Docker

serviceman itself never calls docker. The agent on each machine does — including the machine serviceman runs on, if it is to carry services — so it is the agent that needs an account in the docker group, or DOCKER_HOST pointing at a socket it may use.

#serviceman in a container, with tailscale inside

Dockerfile builds serviceman together with a tailscale agent, for a machine that should carry neither. There is no docker command in the image: the containers of a service are started by the agent on the machine that is meant to carry them.

bin/build            # docker build -t serviceman .
bin/run              # the repo as the source, on the machine's own network, in front of you

bin/run is the one to work with: --rm, no daemon, the image as bin/build built it, with this repo's data/ mounted at /app/data, so its config and its logs stay between runs. The image holds node, tailscale, the packages and the source: change any of those and it wants bin/build again. TS_AUTHKEY is taken from your environment when it is set. demos/docker-compose.yml is the same image left running on a machine instead.

The container keeps a network of its own. Two ports are published on the machine's loopback and nothing else — 3000 for the services, 3001 for the control page — so nothing is open on the machine's public address. tailscaled joins the tailnet from inside and hands the connections it receives to 127.0.0.1 in the container, so a tailnet peer reaches serviceman and nothing else on the machine. --net host would make that loopback the machine's own, and then any port on the machine would be a port on the tailnet.

Its config is data/serviceman.json, on the volume beside the logs and the secrets. bin/configure writes a starting one when there is none, and a first run of the image does the same when it finds none, with the two things below set; the file belongs to whoever owns data/, not to root, and it is yours from then on. A path in it means what it means on the machine that carries the service: serviceman in here runs nothing itself.

The tailnet is a way in, and a proxy is the way out. tailscaled runs in userspace mode, so nothing serviceman dials goes through it: from in here a tailnet address is not routed and a tailnet name does not resolve. tailscaled also runs a proxy on the container's own localhost:1055, published nowhere, and TAILNET_PROXY points serviceman at it. Its calls to Logline go that way, so Logline's address may be a tailnet IP or a *.ts.net name. Nothing else serviceman does uses it.

Each build takes the newest tailscale. The binaries come from the tailscale/tailscale:stable image, and bin/build builds with --pull, so every build fetches the newest stable release, and the newest node:24-alpine, for the machine's own architecture.

Three things follow from that network, and the image handles all three:

A published port does not arrive on the container's loopback. So both doors bind 0.0.0.0 inside, where docker forwards to. What may reach them is decided outside, by -p 127.0.0.1:... on the machine.

The control page is exposed. A forwarded request is a stranger to serviceman, however local it was on the machine, and without exposed the control page answers 404 to strangers. Its wall is the 127.0.0.1 in -p 127.0.0.1:3001:3001. Take exposed out of the config to have the control page over the tailnet only — those connections do arrive on the loopback in here, so they are let in.

An agent on the machine reaches it through a socket, not a port. The socket is a file, and a file in the container is nowhere — so mount the folder it should live in and point control.socket at it:

docker run … -v $HOME/repos:/repos …            # added to the docker run in bin/run
"control": {"socket": "/repos/serviceman.sock", "socket_mode": "0666"}

Then an agent anywhere on that machine — in another container with the same folder mounted, or on the machine itself — dials --url unix:///…/serviceman.sock and no port is opened for it. The socket is made by root inside the container, so 0600 would refuse an agent running as anybody else; the folder above it is the real gate, and ~/repos is not a folder strangers walk through. That agent is what carries the services of this machine — serviceman in here starts nothing itself, so it needs no docker socket and no docker command.

Volume What is in it
/app/data serviceman.json, the config; the logs, tailscaled's in tailscaled.log; the secrets
a folder of yours Where the control socket lands, for agents on the machine
/var/lib/tailscale The tailscale identity of this machine. Keep it.
/var/run/serviceman The control socket, for an agent on the machine itself
Variable What it does
TS_AUTHKEY Joins the tailnet with no hands. Without it, docker logs has the link.
SERVICEMAN_OWNER_TOKEN The owner's token of the control page, instead of data/owner.token.

bin/run hands these two to docker by name, from your environment, so neither value stands on its command line; a container's environment is still readable by whoever may run docker inspect, so prefer data/owner.token, made by serviceman and readable by you alone, over SERVICEMAN_OWNER_TOKEN. | TS_HOSTNAME | The name on the tailnet. Default serviceman. | | TS_SERVE | 1 puts tailscale serve in front, so the address is https. | | TS_EXTRA_ARGS | More for tailscale up — --advertise-tags=tag:server, and the rest. |

A first run writes data/serviceman.json if there is none; after that the file is yours and nothing here writes over it. Every start reads it and says what will not work in a container — a door on the loopback, a control page that is not exposed, a control socket nothing outside can open.

One thing worth deciding. The control page answers on the tailnet like everything else, so everyone on your tailnet can open it — "control": {"port": null} leaves it on its socket only. The services of the machine itself are the agent's to run: it needs only node and docker, and it dials the control socket in /run/serviceman.

#systemd

[Unit]
Description=serviceman
After=network.target

[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/srv/serviceman
ExecStart=/srv/serviceman/bin/run
Restart=always
User=serviceman

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Restart=always is safe: serviceman adopts the containers that are already running, through the agents that dial in again.

#What is reachable, and by whom

Nothing is open until the config opens it.

Door Bound to Who is answered
The services, listen 127.0.0.1 Anyone who reaches the address.
The services, listen.socket a file Anyone who may open the file.
The control page, control.socket a file Anyone who may open the file, mode 0600.
The control page, control 127.0.0.1 This machine only, over either port.
The remote link, /api/v1/remote with listen Anyone holding that remote's token.
The agent file, /api/v1/agent.js with listen Anyone. It is public code and holds no secret.

To serve the public, widen the service port and put TLS in front:

"listen": {"host": "0.0.0.0", "port": 8080}

The control page stays closed to the outside even then. It starts and stops services, edits the config, holds the remote tokens and opens a shell on every machine with an agent, so it answers the machine serviceman runs on and nobody else. Asked from anywhere else it is a 404, over either port, exactly like an address no service claims.

#A token for every caller

Even on this machine, and through the control socket, nothing gets in without a token:

  • The owner's token may do everything. serviceman makes it the first time it starts and keeps it in data/owner.token, readable by you alone; bin/owner-token prints it. SERVICEMAN_OWNER_TOKEN gives one of your own instead, and then no file is written. The page asks for it once and keeps it in a cookie only its own requests carry: never sent on to a service, and marked Secure when the page came over https; Sign out is DELETE /api/v1/session.
  • An agent's token is made on the page's Tokens tab, for an agent or a program: a label, the machines it sees, and its rights on them. The reads are status, metrics, processes, ports, disks, packages and containers. files is the file manager of its machines within its folders (~/visual-agency, ~/notes, the same on each, ~ that machine's home; the first is where it starts): the machine's agent resolves every path, links included, and refuses whatever lies outside them, so neither ../ nor a link that leads out gets past it. A folder not there yet lists empty and is made by the first write into it. Copies between machines stay the owner's. terminals lists, makes, joins, signals and ends the kept terminals of its machines, a shell on each of them that goes anywhere, so treat such a token like an ssh key to them. versions sends a new version of an app folder on its machines, as a zip (PUT /api/v1/services/<name>/zip, A new version of an app folder): what it sends runs there as the app, so it is a key to those apps; Apps keeps it to the app folders ticked, and a service's page makes one for that service alone, Make a token for …, with the curl line beside it. It is shown once, and only its hash is kept, in data/control_tokens.json. It never touches the config, a secret, another machine, or a service but the one it sends a new version to, and opens no other shell. Edit… changes its label, machines (every machine, those added later too, is one tick), rights, folders and apps in place, the token staying the same; Rotate… gives it a new value, shown once, the old one refused at once; Revoke… ends it.

A caller sends its token with every request:

curl --unix-socket data/serviceman.sock -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost/api/v1/status

An agent's status is its own: its machines and what runs on them, nothing of the config. Every route says which right it needs in one table (control_route_right.js); a route that says none, one added later included, is the owner's alone. The agent file, the installer and an agent dialling in with its remote token need no token of the control door.

Reach it from your laptop with an SSH tunnel:

ssh -L 8081:127.0.0.1:8081 you@the-host

If you would rather put your own wall in front — an authenticating proxy, a VPN — say so:

"control": {"exposed": true, "names": ["ops.example.com"]}

exposed lets other callers in; names adds the hostnames that proxy asks by. serviceman prints a line at startup when exposed is on, so it is never a surprise. Without it, a hostname pointed at 127.0.0.1 by someone else's DNS gets nowhere either: the control page answers its own names only.

Set "control": {"host": null, "port": null} to switch it off completely, or "control": {"shell": false} to keep the page and close the shell door alone.

#The control API

Everything the control page does, it does through these. They all answer this machine only, they all want a token (above), and they all live under /api/v1/ — on the control port, or on the control hostname over the service port.

Call What it does
GET /api/v1/status Every service, every remote, and the log.
GET /navplace Every service with an address, as a NavPlace collection.
GET /api/v1/config The config file as text, with its hash.
POST /api/v1/config/check Read a config and say what is wrong with it.
POST /api/v1/config Write it, and apply it to the running services.
POST /api/v1/services Add a service.
PUT /api/v1/services/<name> Reshape one.
DELETE /api/v1/services/<name> Take one away.
POST /api/v1/services/<name>/start Start it now.
POST /api/v1/services/<name>/restart Stop it, then start it again, as one ask.
POST /api/v1/services/<name>/stop Stop it now.
POST /api/v1/services/<name>/update Fetch the program again, then start it again.
POST /api/v1/services/<name>/pull Fetch the image again; remake what runs on it.

| GET /api/v1/image-ports?image=&remote= | What ports an image says it exposes, asked of that machine's docker. | | POST /api/v1/remotes | Add a remote. | | PUT /api/v1/remotes/<name> | Reshape one. | | DELETE /api/v1/remotes/<name> | Take one away, unless a service names it. | | GET /api/v1/shell?service=&slot= | A websocket into a container. |

Two doors under the same prefix are not part of it: GET /api/v1/agent.js hands the agent to anyone who asks, and GET /api/v1/remote is where an agent dials in with its token.

#What a visitor learns

A visitor whose service is down gets a page that says it did not answer, and nothing else — no ports, no container names, no docker output, no remote names. The reason goes to the log and to callers from this machine. The one address a visitor may poll, /__serviceman__/status.json, answers the phase and how far a start is, and of a failure the same short line as the page, with no output of the program; the reason and the output go to callers from this machine, as the page's do.
